title: Form
intro: Form is how a piece is put together over time: small ideas grouped into phrases, phrases into sections, sections into a whole. This chapter starts with the smallest units and the two classic phrase structures, the period and the sentence.

blocks.text: A motive is the smallest recognisable musical idea, a few notes with a distinct rhythm and contour: the four-note 'short-short-short-long' opening of Beethoven's Fifth Symphony is the most famous. Composers develop motives by repeating them at other pitches (sequence), inverting them, changing their rhythm (augmentation, diminution) or fragmenting them.

A phrase is a complete musical thought that ends with a cadence, typically four bars long (often eight in fast music). The cadence decides how closed it sounds (see Cadences (#/arts/music-theory/harmony/cadences)).

A period joins two phrases as question and answer. The antecedent ends with a weaker cadence (usually a half cadence); the consequent starts the same way and ends with a stronger one (a PAC). If both phrases begin alike it is a parallel period; if not, contrasting. The theme of Mozart's Piano Sonata in A major, K. 331, is a textbook parallel period.

The sentence (Schoenberg's term, refined by Caplin) is an eight-bar theme in two halves: a presentation, a two-bar idea and its repetition (often on V), then a continuation that fragments the idea, speeds up the harmonic rhythm and drives to a cadence. Proportions 2 + 2 + 4: statement, restatement, development and close. The opening of Beethoven's Piano Sonata Op. 2 No. 1 is the standard example.

blocks.text: Themes combine into sections, and sections into forms identified with letters: A for the first section, B for contrasting material, A′ for a varied return.

items: Classical Forms (#/arts/music-theory/form/classical-forms): binary, ternary, rondo, theme and variations, sonata form.
Popular Forms (#/arts/music-theory/form/popular-forms): the 12-bar blues, 32-bar AABA, verse–chorus.

blocks.text: Analyse with the score open: mark each cadence, then group phrases by their cadences. Then play the piece's skeleton, just the bass and melody at each cadence; the form becomes audible without the decoration.

blocks.title: Period or sentence
blocks.text: An eight-bar theme: bars 1–2 a basic idea on I, bars 3–4 the same idea on V, bars 5–8 shorter fragments leading to a PAC. Period or sentence?
solution: A repeated two-bar idea followed by a four-bar continuation that fragments and cadences is a sentence (presentation 2 + 2, continuation 4).
